A gradiometer system including one or more magnetic sensor(s) is disclosed. The gradiometer includes an actuation module connectable to the magnetic sensor(s) to vary one or more sensing positions at which a magnetic field is sensed thereby. The one or more sensing positions are varied according to a certain displacement function indicating a predetermined displacement between the sensing positions as a function of time. A controller of the gradiometer system is adapted to determine at least one vector component of a gradient of the magnetic field sensed by the sensor(s) by carrying out the following: (i) obtaining readout data from the sensor(s) indicative of the magnetic field sensed at the varied sensing positions during a certain measurement time duration; (ii) processing the readout data to determine a differential magnetic field time profile indicating a difference between the magnetic fields sensed at at least two of the sensing positions during the measurement time duration; and (iii) demodulating the differential magnetic field time profile in accordance with the displacement function to thereby determine a demodulated time profile indicative of the at least one vector component of the gradient of the measured magnetic field.

A gradiometer system is described that uses one or more magnetic sensors. The gradiometer has an actuation module that can be coupled to the magnetic sensor or sensors in order to change one or more sensing locations where the magnetic field is detected. These sensing locations are adjusted according to a defined displacement function, which specifies a preselected separation between the sensing positions over time.

A controller in the gradiometer system is configured to calculate at least one vector component of the gradient of the magnetic field measured by the sensor or sensors. To do this, the controller: (i) receives readout data from the sensor or sensors representing the magnetic field detected at the changing sensing locations over a specified measurement period; (ii) analyzes the readout data to derive a differential magnetic-field time profile that represents the difference between magnetic fields measured at two or more of the sensing locations during that measurement period; and (iii) demodulates the differential magnetic-field time profile based on the displacement function, producing a demodulated time profile that represents the at least one vector component of the gradient of the measured magnetic field.

A gradiometer system may include one or more magnetic sensors configured to sense a magnetic field. The magnetic sensors may be arranged to generate sensor readout data representative of the magnetic field at respective sensing positions.

The gradiometer system further includes an actuation module configured to vary the sensing positions of the magnetic sensors over time. In particular, the actuation module may displace one or more of the magnetic sensors relative to a reference position, relative to one another, or relative to a magnetic-field source or measurement region. The displacement of the sensing positions is performed according to a predetermined displacement function, where the predetermined displacement function defines displacement as a function of time.

During a measurement time duration, a controller obtains sensor readout data from the magnetic sensors while the sensing positions are being varied. As a result, the sensor readout data corresponds to magnetic-field measurements taken at different spatial positions over time. The controller may associate the sensor readout data with the corresponding sensing positions defined by the predetermined displacement function.

The controller then processes the sensor readout data to determine a differential magnetic field profile. The differential magnetic field profile represents variations in the sensed magnetic field as a function of the controlled displacement of the sensing positions. The controller demodulates the differential magnetic field profile using information associated with the predetermined displacement function. Based on the demodulated differential magnetic field profile, the controller determines at least one vector component of the magnetic field gradient. In this manner, the gradiometer system can derive gradient information from time-varying sensor position measurements rather than relying solely on fixed spatial separation between sensors.
outputs.L4:
A gradiometer system may include one or more magnetic field sensors arranged to detect a magnetic field at different sensing positions over time. The system further includes an actuation module configured to vary the position of at least one sensing element according to a predetermined time-dependent displacement function. In this way, rather than relying only on a fixed spatial separation between two static sensors, the system dynamically changes the location at which magnetic field measurements are obtained. The displacement may be periodic, oscillatory, linear, rotational, or otherwise controlled so that the sensor position is known as a function of time.

A controller is coupled to the magnetic sensor or sensors and to the actuation module. The controller may command or monitor the motion produced by the actuation module and may acquire magnetic field readout data corresponding to the different sensing positions. The acquired data may include time-varying magnetic field measurements that reflect both the spatial variation of the external magnetic field and the imposed movement of the sensor. Because the displacement function is predetermined or otherwise known, the controller can associate each magnetic field measurement with a corresponding sensor position.

The controller processes the magnetic field readout data to derive a differential magnetic field time profile. This profile represents changes in the measured magnetic field caused by the controlled displacement of the sensing position. The differential profile may be obtained by comparing measurements from multiple sensors, by subtracting measurements taken at different times or positions, or by extracting the portion of the sensor output that corresponds to the imposed displacement.

The controller then demodulates the differential magnetic field time profile using information associated with the displacement function. For example, if the sensor is moved sinusoidally, the controller may demodulate the magnetic field response at the same frequency and phase as the imposed displacement. This demodulation separates the field-gradient-related signal from background fields, offsets, low-frequency drift, or other noise components. The resulting demodulated signal is proportional to one or more spatial derivatives of the magnetic field.

From the demodulated differential magnetic field time profile, the system determines vector components of the magnetic field gradient. These components may correspond to gradients along one or more spatial axes, depending on the direction and form of the sensor displacement. By selecting suitable displacement functions, the system may measure gradient components in a single direction, in multiple orthogonal directions, or in a more complex spatial pattern. The gradient information may be represented as one or more elements of a magnetic field gradient tensor.

Accordingly, the gradiometer system enables magnetic field gradient measurement using dynamically varied sensor positions. This approach can reduce dependence on precisely matched static sensor pairs, improve rejection of common-mode magnetic field signals, and allow flexible measurement of magnetic field gradients using controlled sensor motion and signal processing matched to the known displacement function.

**The Power of “The”**

“The” is one of the smallest words in English, yet it is also one of the most important. It is called the definite article, and it helps us point to something specific. When we say “a book,” we may mean any book. But when we say “the book,” we are talking about a particular book that the speaker and listener already know about.

This simple word gives clarity and direction to sentences. It can make an idea feel more exact, more familiar, or more important. For example, “the sun,” “the world,” and “the future” all refer to things that feel known or unique. Without “the,” English would often sound incomplete or unclear.

Although it may seem ordinary, “the” plays a powerful role in communication. It connects people through shared understanding and helps language become more precise. Sometimes, the smallest words carry the greatest meaning.

**Abstract**

A system and method are provided for determining a magnetic field gradient using one or more mechanically actuated magnetic sensors. A magnetic sensor is displaced between at least two spatial positions within a magnetic field while magnetic field measurements are recorded over a measurement duration. The recorded measurements are used to form a differential time profile representative of a difference in magnetic field between the spatial positions. The differential time profile is demodulated, for example based on an actuation frequency or timing of the mechanical displacement, to determine a magnetic field gradient. Mechanical actuation of the sensor enables gradient determination with reduced sensitivity to common-mode field variations, sensor offset, and low-frequency noise, and may be used in magnetic sensing, navigation, current sensing, geophysical sensing, biomedical sensing, or other applications requiring spatial magnetic field information.

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a formal invention description for a magnetic gradiometer system including sensors, an actuation module, predetermined time-dependent displacement between sensing locations, and controller-based processing to extract gradient vector components.
counterfactuals.output:
## Invention Description: Magnetic Gradiometer System with Time-Dependent Sensor Displacement

### Field of the Invention

The present invention relates generally to magnetic sensing systems and, more particularly, to magnetic gradiometers configured to determine spatial gradients of a magnetic field using controlled relative displacement between magnetic sensing locations and controller-based signal processing.

### Background

Magnetic gradiometers are used to measure spatial variations of magnetic fields and are useful in navigation, geophysical surveying, anomaly detection, biomedical sensing, and industrial inspection. Conventional gradiometers commonly employ multiple magnetic sensors arranged at fixed spatial separations. The accuracy of such systems may be limited by sensor mismatch, alignment tolerances, fixed baseline geometry, thermal drift, and common-mode magnetic noise.

There is a need for a magnetic gradiometer system capable of extracting magnetic field gradient components using known, time-dependent displacement between sensing locations, thereby enabling improved calibration, configurable gradient sensitivity, and enhanced rejection of common-mode effects.

### Summary of the Invention

A magnetic gradiometer system is provided. The system includes one or more magnetic sensors defining magnetic sensing locations, an actuation module configured to produce a predetermined time-dependent displacement between at least two sensing locations, and a controller configured to receive magnetic field measurements from the sensors and process the measurements in view of the known displacement to extract one or more components of a magnetic field gradient vector.

In one embodiment, the magnetic gradiometer includes a first magnetic sensor associated with a first sensing location and a second magnetic sensor associated with a second sensing location. The actuation module changes the relative position of the first and second sensing locations according to a predetermined displacement function. The controller determines a difference between magnetic field measurements obtained at the sensing locations and computes at least one spatial derivative of the magnetic field based on the difference and the displacement function.

In another embodiment, a single magnetic sensor is displaced relative to a reference frame so that the sensor samples a magnetic field at a plurality of time-varying sensing locations. The controller correlates the measured magnetic field signal with the predetermined displacement waveform to derive gradient vector components.

### Detailed Description

The magnetic gradiometer system comprises a sensor assembly including at least one magnetic field sensor. The magnetic field sensor may include, without limitation, a magnetoresistive sensor, fluxgate sensor, Hall-effect sensor, optically pumped magnetometer, superconducting quantum interference device, search-coil sensor, nitrogen-vacancy center magnetometer, or any other device capable of generating a signal representative of a magnetic field or a component thereof.

The sensor assembly defines at least two sensing locations. The sensing locations may be associated with physically separate sensors, separate sensitive volumes within a common sensor package, or different positions of a movable sensor at different times. Each sensing location is characterized by a position in a coordinate frame associated with the gradiometer system.

The system further includes an actuation module mechanically, piezoelectrically, electrostatically, magnetically, pneumatically, hydraulically, thermally, or otherwise coupled to at least a portion of the sensor assembly. The actuation module is configured to impose a predetermined time-dependent displacement between the sensing locations. The displacement may be translational, rotational, oscillatory, reciprocating, periodic, quasi-periodic, stepped, chirped, or otherwise time-varying. In some embodiments, the displacement is represented by a known displacement vector:

\[
\Delta \mathbf{r}(t)=\mathbf{r}_2(t)-\mathbf{r}_1(t)
\]

where \(\mathbf{r}_1(t)\) and \(\mathbf{r}_2(t)\) are positions of first and second sensing locations.

The actuation module may include one or more actuators configured to move one sensor relative to another, move a common sensor support relative to an external magnetic field, modulate the baseline between sensors, or rotate the sensor assembly. The predetermined displacement may be stored in memory, generated by a waveform generator, measured by a position sensor, or controlled by feedback. In certain embodiments, the displacement is selected to provide sensitivity to a desired gradient component or to separate gradient signals from offset, drift, and environmental noise.

The controller is operatively coupled to the magnetic sensor or sensors and to the actuation module. The controller may include one or more processors, microcontrollers, digital signal processors, field-programmable gate arrays, analog circuits, mixed-signal circuits, memory devices, timing circuits, and communication interfaces. The controller is configured to receive sensor signals corresponding to magnetic field measurements acquired at the sensing locations and to process the received signals using information indicative of the predetermined displacement.

For two sensing locations, the controller may determine a magnetic field difference:

\[
\Delta \mathbf{B}(t)=\mathbf{B}(\mathbf{r}_2(t),t)-\mathbf{B}(\mathbf{r}_1(t),t)
\]

and estimate a magnetic field gradient tensor or one or more components thereof. For sufficiently small displacement, the difference may be approximated as:

\[
\Delta \mathbf{B}(t)\approx \nabla \mathbf{B}(\mathbf{r}_1,t)\,\Delta \mathbf{r}(t)
\]

where \(\nabla \mathbf{B}\) represents the magnetic field gradient tensor. If the sensor measures a scalar field magnitude or a selected vector component, the controller may compute corresponding directional derivatives along the displacement direction.

In one implementation, where a magnetic field component \(B_i\) is measured and the displacement has a component along coordinate direction \(x_j\), the controller estimates:

\[
\frac{\partial B_i}{\partial x_j}\approx \frac{B_i(\mathbf{r}+\Delta \mathbf{r},t)-B_i(\mathbf{r},t)}{\Delta r_j}
\]

or obtains the gradient component by fitting, demodulating, or correlating the measured magnetic signal with the known time-dependent displacement waveform.

Where the displacement is oscillatory, for example:

\[
\Delta \mathbf{r}(t)=\mathbf{a}\sin(\omega t+\phi)
\]

the controller may extract the gradient contribution by lock-in detection at the actuation frequency \(\omega\). The amplitude and phase of the magnetic signal component synchronous with the displacement are used to determine the projection of the magnetic gradient along the displacement vector. By using multiple displacement directions, multiple frequencies, multiple phases, or multiple actuators, the controller may determine two or more independent components of the gradient vector or gradient tensor.

The controller may further perform calibration, filtering, synchronization, compensation for sensor scale factors, compensation for sensor offsets, compensation for actuator nonlinearity, temperature correction, rejection of common-mode magnetic fields, and estimation of uncertainty. The controller may also use position feedback from an encoder, interferometer, capacitive sensor, strain gauge, accelerometer, or other displacement sensor to determine the actual displacement as a function of time.

In some embodiments, the system includes three-axis magnetic sensors at one or more sensing locations. The controller may use measurements of the vector magnetic field and a plurality of known displacement vectors to solve for gradient vector components in a coordinate system fixed to the sensor assembly or in an external reference frame. The resulting gradient information may be output as one or more of: a scalar gradient magnitude, a directional derivative, a gradient vector, a magnetic field gradient tensor, a compensated magnetic anomaly signal, or navigation information.

The predetermined time-dependent displacement may be selected to improve signal-to-noise ratio by shifting gradient information to a frequency band having reduced low-frequency sensor drift. The displacement may also be selected to allow differential measurement using a single sensor moved between two or more positions, thereby reducing errors caused by mismatch between separate sensors. Alternatively, multiple sensors may be actuated in a coordinated manner to increase bandwidth or enable simultaneous measurement of several gradient components.

### Example Embodiment

In an exemplary embodiment, a magnetic gradiometer system includes first and second three-axis magnetometers mounted on respective movable supports. A piezoelectric actuator is coupled to at least one support and is driven by a controller to create a sinusoidal baseline variation between the magnetometers along a known axis. The controller samples the magnetometer outputs synchronously with the actuator drive signal. The controller subtracts corresponding magnetic field components measured by the two magnetometers and demodulates the resulting difference signal at the actuator frequency. Based on the known displacement amplitude and direction, the controller computes at least one magnetic gradient component, such as \(\partial B_x/\partial x\), \(\partial B_y/\partial x\), or \(\partial B_z/\partial x\). By repeating the actuation along different axes, or by employing multiple actuators driven at distinct frequencies, the controller determines additional gradient vector or tensor components.

### Advantages

The disclosed magnetic gradiometer system provides one or more advantages, including configurable baseline length, improved rejection of sensor offsets and drift, extraction of gradient components by synchronous processing, reduced dependence on fixed mechanical tolerances, and the ability to determine multiple gradient components using predetermined sensor displacement. The system may be implemented using a single moving sensor or multiple sensors and may be adapted for compact, high-sensitivity magnetic field gradient measurements in stationary or mobile platforms.
